opus-5.5.text:
I think the strongest agent isn't defined by a single benchmark score. It's defined by how much of the world it can actually interact with, and how well it learns from that interaction.

Most people picture a smarter chatbot, something that answers harder questions. But answering questions is a small part of what intelligence does. The more interesting question is whether it can take actions in an open-ended environment over a long horizon, and whether those actions create real value.

There are a few dimensions I'd look at.

**Breadth of environment.** Early agents lived in games or very narrow settings. Language models changed that, because language is a general interface. Now an agent can use a computer, browse the web, write and run code, and call tools. The strongest agent can operate in essentially any environment a human can operate in digitally, and maybe eventually physically.

**Length of horizon.** Today's agents are pretty good at tasks that take a few minutes. The frontier is tasks that take hours, days, maybe weeks: running a research project, building a product, managing a complex workflow. That requires memory, planning, and the ability to recover from mistakes, not just being right on the first step.

**Learning from experience.** This is the part I find most important and most underexplored. Humans get better the longer they do a job. Right now, models are mostly frozen after training. Every time you open a new session, it's a bit like talking to someone with amnesia. The strongest agent would accumulate context, knowledge, and skills from its own experience, and keep improving on the specific things you care about.

**Interaction with people.** Intelligence isn't only about solving a problem on its own. A lot of real work is about understanding what someone actually wants, which is often underspecified, and collaborating with them. So I'd also judge an agent by how well it works with humans, not just how autonomous it is.

If I put it simply: the strongest agent is one that can be dropped into almost any environment, given a fuzzy, long-term goal, and over time it figures things out, gets better, and delivers real value, the way a very capable new colleague would. We're not there yet. But I think the path is less about making models better at exams and more about defining the right tasks, the right environments, and the right ways to measure utility in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response ties an agent’s strength to how broadly it can interact with environments and learn through those interactions, rather than to benchmark scores alone.

r002.rationale: It says people tend to imagine AI as a smarter chatbot answering harder questions, then argues that this question-answering view misses much of intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about the strongest AI agent, I actually try not to start from a picture of some superhuman thing. I start from a very simple definition: an agent is something that takes actions in an environment, gets feedback, and uses that feedback to achieve a goal. Language models gave us a new kind of agent, one where the "actions" are words, so the agent can think, use tools, talk to people, all through the same interface. That was the intuition behind ReAct and later SWE-agent, and it still shapes how I imagine the endpoint.

So the strongest agent, to me, has three properties.

First, it's general. Not general in the sense of "it can do a thousand benchmarks," but general in the sense that you can drop it into a new environment with a new set of tools and a new goal, and it figures out the interface on its own. Today most agents are still quite tied to their scaffolds. We hand-design the tool set, the prompt, the loop. The strongest agent shouldn't need that. It should treat the scaffold as part of the environment and learn it.

Second, it learns from experience over long horizons. Right now a model is mostly fixed after training, and an "agent" is that frozen model wrapped in a loop. That's a bit strange if you think about it. A person who works in a company for a year is much more useful in month twelve than in month one, not because their brain changed architecture, but because they accumulated context, mistakes, intuitions. The strongest agent has to close that loop, whether through memory, through continual learning, or through RL on its own trajectories. I think this is where the real gap is. Reasoning is improving quickly. Learning from your own long-horizon experience is still mostly unsolved.

Third, and this is the part people underrate, it has the right environments and the right feedback. I've said before that I think we're in the second half of AI, where the bottleneck is less about new methods and more about defining the right problems and the right ways to measure progress. An agent is only as strong as the environments it was trained in and the signals it got there. If you give a model a clean, verifiable task like coding with tests, it gets very good. If you give it a messy, real-world task where success is ambiguous, progress is slow. So part of imagining the strongest agent is imagining the training environments that would produce it: realistic, diverse, with reward that reflects what people actually care about, not proxies.

If I put that together, the image in my head is not a robot or a single chat window. It's something more like a very good colleague who lives in your computer. You give it a goal in plain language, it works for hours or days, uses whatever tools exist, asks you when it's genuinely uncertain, and it gets better the longer it works with you. It doesn't need a new prompt engineering trick every time the task changes.

And honestly, I think the hardest part isn't intelligence in the narrow sense. It's utility. Models are already smarter than most tasks require. The question is whether we can make them reliably useful in environments that aren't designed for them. The strongest agent is the one that closes that gap, and I think the path there runs through environments and evaluation as much as through models.

r001.rationale: The response describes language models’ word-based actions and says agents should adapt to new tools, but it does not state that an agent’s intelligence ceiling depends on its mode of interaction.

r002.rationale: The response critiques agents’ dependence on designed scaffolds and rejects imagining the endpoint as a robot or chat window. It does not say that current imagination about AI is constrained by inherited modes of interaction.

astra-6.text:
I imagine an agent that can take a high-level goal and figure out how to achieve it, even when the path isn’t clear at the beginning. It can learn about its environment, make a plan, take actions, and use feedback to revise that plan. If it gets stuck, it can recognize what it’s missing—whether that’s information, a tool, or help from a human.

For me, the interesting part is how much complexity you can delegate to it. Answering a question is one thing. Working on a difficult problem for days or weeks, checking whether you’re making progress, and recovering from mistakes is a much bigger challenge. The strongest agent would be able to sustain that process while staying aligned with what you actually wanted.

And it wouldn’t necessarily do everything independently. Knowing when to ask you a question could be a sign of intelligence. You’d give it a goal, and you could trust both its ability to pursue that goal and its judgment about when to bring you back into the loop.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent’s abilities and when it should involve a human, but does not say its intelligence ceiling depends on its mode of interaction.

r002.rationale: The response does not observe that inherited interaction modes constrain how people imagine AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I imagine the strongest agent as a system that can take a high-level goal and figure out how to achieve it, even when the path isn’t clear in advance. It can reason, use tools, learn from feedback, and keep making progress over a long period of time. And when it gets stuck, it can recognize what’s missing—whether that’s information, a capability, or a decision from a human.

For me, the interesting part is the relationship between intelligence and the environment. An agent doesn’t have to hold everything in its context or solve everything through internal reasoning. It can write things down, run experiments, build tools, and change its environment to make future steps easier. So the strongest agent might look less like a chatbot that gives a brilliant answer and more like a researcher who gradually turns an unclear problem into something they can solve.

But I wouldn’t define strength just by how independently it acts. It also needs good judgment about when to ask for help and whether it’s pursuing the right goal. Being very capable at achieving the wrong objective isn’t what we want.

r001.rationale: The response links intelligence to interaction with the environment, describing how an agent can use tools, experiments, and environmental changes to make progress.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a chatbot with a researcher, but does not say that current ideas about AI are constrained by inherited modes of interaction.
